ch15.title: Corinth and Athens
ch15.b002: When the time came to leave Rome, Jesus said good-bye to none of his friends. The scribe of Damascus had appeared in the city without announcement, and he disappeared in the same way. It was a full year before those who had known and loved him gave up hope of seeing him again. Before the end of the second year, small groups of them found themselves drawn together by a common interest in what he had taught and by the shared memory of good times spent in his company. These little gatherings of Stoics, Cynics, and mystery cultists went on meeting, irregular and informal, right up to the day when the first preachers of the Christian religion appeared in Rome.
ch15.b003: Gonod and Ganid had bought so many things in Alexandria and Rome that they sent all their belongings ahead by pack train to Tarentum, and the three travelers walked at their leisure down the length of Italy on the great Appian Way. Along it they met every sort of human being. Many noble Roman citizens and Greek colonists lived beside this road, but already the progeny of great numbers of inferior slaves were beginning to appear among them. One day, resting at lunch about halfway to Tarentum, Ganid asked Jesus directly what he thought of India’s caste system. Jesus answered that though human beings differ in many ways, before God and in the spiritual world all mortals stand on an equal footing. “⟦Q 133:0.3⟧There are only two groups of mortals in the eyes of God: those who desire to do his will and those who do not.⟦/Q⟧” Mankind may be divided into many classes, but before the judgment bar of God they stand as equals, and “⟦Q 133:0.3⟧you should make no such distinctions in the spiritual brotherhood of men when assembled for worship in the presence of God.⟦/Q⟧”
ch15.b005: As they neared Tarentum one afternoon, something happened by the roadside. A rough and bullying youth was brutally attacking a smaller lad. Jesus hurried to the rescue, and when he had freed the boy, he held tightly to the offender until the smaller lad had made his escape. The moment Jesus let go, Ganid pounced on the young bully and began soundly to thrash him, and to Ganid’s astonishment Jesus promptly stopped him. The frightened boy ran off down the road. As soon as Ganid had his breath again, he exclaimed: “⟦Q 133:1.1⟧I cannot understand you, Teacher. If mercy requires that you rescue the smaller lad, does not justice demand the punishment of the larger and offending youth?⟦/Q⟧”
ch15.b006: Jesus answered him quietly. “⟦Q 133:1.2⟧Ganid, it is true, you do not understand. Mercy ministry is always the work of the individual, but justice punishment is the function of the social, governmental, or universe administrative groups.⟦/Q⟧” As an individual he was bound to show mercy, and so he had restrained the aggressor until the weaker boy could get away; but he had not sat in judgment on the attacker or punished him. “⟦Q 133:1.2⟧Ganid, mercy may be lavish, but justice is precise.⟦/Q⟧” No two persons are likely to agree on what punishment would satisfy justice; one would impose forty lashes, another twenty, a third solitary confinement. Such responsibilities had better rest with the group, and in the universe with those who fully know the antecedents of all wrongdoing as well as its motivation.
ch15.b007: For days they talked about this problem of showing mercy and administering justice, and Ganid came to understand, at least in part, why Jesus would not engage in personal combat. But he asked one last question, to which he never received a fully satisfactory answer: “⟦Q 133:1.3⟧But, Teacher, if a stronger and ill-tempered creature should attack you and threaten to destroy you, what would you do? Would you make no effort to defend yourself?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus could not answer fully, for he was not willing to reveal that he was living on earth as the exemplification of the Paradise Father’s love to an onlooking universe. He did say this much: if he judged that an attacker did not possess moral judgment and spiritual reason, he would defend himself without hesitation. But he would not assault a fellow man of sonship status, even in self-defense; he would not punish him in advance and without judgment. He would use every possible means to prevent and dissuade such an attack, and to soften it if he failed. “⟦Q 133:1.4⟧I am absolutely assured that the entire universe is friendly to me—this all-powerful truth I insist on believing with a wholehearted trust in spite of all appearances to the contrary.⟦/Q⟧”
ch15.b008: Ganid was still not fully satisfied. When Jesus told him about Jacob the stone mason’s son, who had appointed himself Jesus’ defender, the lad decided that someone would always be on hand to defend so kindly a man. Jesus replied simply: “⟦Q 133:1.5⟧That test has not yet come, Ganid, and when it does, we will have to abide by the Father’s will.⟦/Q⟧” That was about all the lad could get his teacher to say on self-defense and nonresistance, though on another occasion Jesus did grant that organized society had every right to use force in carrying out its just mandates.
ch15.b010: At Tarentum, while they waited on the landing for the boat to unload its cargo, the travelers saw a man mistreating his wife. As was his custom, Jesus intervened on behalf of the one under attack. He stepped up behind the angry husband, tapped him gently on the shoulder, and said: “⟦Q 133:2.1⟧My friend, may I speak with you in private for a moment?⟦/Q⟧” The man, thrown off balance by such an approach, stammered that he supposed so. Jesus led him aside and asked what could have happened to so strong a man to make him attack his wife, the mother of his children, right out before all eyes. He said he thought he could see in the man’s face the love of justice. It was not so much what Jesus said that touched the man’s heart as the kindly look and the sympathetic smile he gave him at the end. The man took him for a priest of the Cynics. His wife had done no great wrong, he confessed; she was a good woman, but she irritated him by picking on him in public, and he lost his temper. He was sorry for his lack of self-control, and he promised to do better.
ch15.b011: In bidding him farewell, Jesus said: “⟦Q 133:2.2⟧My brother, always remember that man has no rightful authority over woman unless the woman has willingly and voluntarily given him such authority.⟦/Q⟧” His wife carried the far greater share of bearing and rearing their children, and it was only fair that she receive his special protection. “⟦Q 133:2.2⟧Do you not know that men and women are partners with God in that they co-operate to create beings who grow up to possess themselves of the potential of immortal souls?⟦/Q⟧” If the man could love his children as God loved him, he would love and cherish his wife as the Father in heaven honors and exalts the Infinite Spirit, the mother of all the spirit children of a vast universe. As the travelers went on board, they looked back and saw the couple standing together in silent embrace, their eyes wet with tears. Gonod had heard the latter half of Jesus’ words, and all that day he was occupied with them. He resolved to reorganize his own home when he returned to India.
ch15.b012: By Way of Nicopolis to Corinth
ch15.b013: The voyage to Nicopolis was pleasant but slow, for the wind was not favorable. The three spent long hours remembering all that had happened since they first met in Jerusalem. Ganid was becoming imbued with the spirit of personal ministry, and he began to work on the steward of the ship; but on the second day, when he got into deep religious water, he called on Joshua to help him out. They spent several days at Nicopolis, the “city of victory” that Augustus had founded some fifty years before to commemorate the battle of Actium, on the very ground where he had camped with his army. They lodged with Jeramy, a Greek proselyte of the Jewish faith whom they had met on shipboard; in that same house, years later, the Apostle Paul spent a whole winter with Jeramy’s son during his third missionary journey. Then they sailed on in the same boat to Corinth, capital of the Roman province of Achaia.
ch15.b014: Next to Alexandria and Rome, Corinth was the most cosmopolitan city of the Mediterranean world. By now Ganid had become much interested in the Jewish religion, and one day, as they passed the synagogue and saw the people going in, he asked Jesus to take him to the service. They heard a learned rabbi discourse on the “Destiny of Israel,” and afterward they met Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue. Ganid grew very fond of Crispus, his wife, and their five children, and he loved to watch how a Jew conducted his family life. At first he was shocked, and later charmed, by the status of woman in the Jewish home; it was a revelation to the young Indian. Meanwhile Jesus held more than twenty sessions with this forward-looking Jew, teaching him the better ways of religious living. It is not surprising that years afterward, when the Jews had voted to forbid Paul’s preaching in this very synagogue and he had turned to the gentiles, Crispus with his entire family embraced the new religion and became one of the chief supports of the Christian church in Corinth.
ch15.b016: Jesus and Ganid were often guests in another Jewish home, that of Justus, a devout merchant who lived alongside the synagogue. In Rome Ganid had noticed that Jesus would not accompany them to the public baths, and several times afterward he had tried to draw his teacher out on the relations of the sexes; Jesus answered his questions but never seemed disposed to discuss such subjects at length. One evening, as they strolled out near where the wall of the citadel ran down to the sea, two public women accosted them. Ganid had rightly understood that Jesus was a man of high ideals who abhorred everything unclean, and so he spoke sharply to the women and rudely motioned them away. Jesus said to him: “⟦Q 133:3.6⟧You mean well, but you should not presume thus to speak to the children of God, even though they chance to be his erring children. Who are we that we should sit in judgment on these women?⟦/Q⟧” The women were even more astonished at his words than Ganid was.
ch15.b017: As they stood there in the moonlight, Jesus went on. Within every human mind, he said, there lives a divine spirit, the gift of the Father in heaven, ever striving to lead us to God; yet men and women often become confused as they struggle to make a living in a world so largely dominated by selfishness and sin. Neither of these women was willfully wicked. Their faces showed much sorrow; they had not chosen this life on purpose, but in discouragement bordering on despair had surrendered to the pressure of the hour. “⟦Q 133:3.7⟧But, tell me, as you look into these now tear-stained faces, do you see anything bad or wicked?⟦/Q⟧” Ganid’s voice choked as he stammered out his answer: “⟦Q 133:3.7⟧No, Teacher, I do not. And I apologize for my rudeness to them—I crave their forgiveness.⟦/Q⟧” Then said Jesus: “⟦Q 133:3.7⟧And I bespeak for them that they have forgiven you as I speak for my Father in heaven that he has forgiven them. Now all of you come with me to a friend’s house where we will seek refreshment and plan for the new and better life ahead.⟦/Q⟧” The amazed women had not yet uttered a word. They looked at each other and silently followed.
ch15.b018: Imagine the surprise of Martha, the wife of Justus, when at that late hour Jesus appeared at her door with Ganid and two strangers. He asked her pardon for the hour and said he hoped she would help them think how these women, who also needed food, might get a new start in life. When Martha had spread the food on the table, Jesus unexpectedly took his leave: it was late, and the young man’s father would be waiting. He left the three women together, “⟦Q 133:3.9⟧the beloved children of the Most High,⟦/Q⟧” and promised to pray for their guidance while they made plans for a new and better life on earth and eternal life in the great beyond. For a few moments Martha was as speechless as the others, but presently she rose to the occasion and did everything for the strangers that Jesus had hoped. The elder of the two women died not long afterward, with bright hopes of eternal survival. The younger worked at Justus’ place of business and later became a lifelong member of the first Christian church in Corinth.
ch15.b020: During those two months in Corinth, Jesus and Ganid held intimate conversations with scores of worth-while people, and more than half of those so touched later became members of the Christian community. Several times in the home of Crispus they met one Gaius, who afterward became a loyal supporter of Paul. When Paul first came to Corinth, he did not intend to stay long. But he did not know how well the way had been prepared by the “⟦Q 133:3.3⟧Jewish tutor of the son of an Indian merchant,⟦/Q⟧” and he found that great interest had already been aroused by Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish refugees from Rome; Aquila was one of the Cynics whom Jesus had met in that city. Paul lived and worked with these fellow tentmakers and prolonged his stay. Many times, in the home of Justus, he listened to the story of the Indian lad and his Jewish tutor, and both he and Justus wondered whatever had become of so wise and brilliant a Hebrew teacher.
ch15.b021: To each person he met, Jesus spoke a fitting word. He taught the miller to grind the grains of truth in the mill of living experience, so that even the weak could receive the difficult things of divine life. To the Roman centurion he said: “⟦Q 133:4.3⟧Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s and unto God the things which are God’s.⟦/Q⟧” He reminded the earnest leader of the Mithraic cult that the mystery of eternal salvation dwelt within his own soul, and he urged the Roman judge to “judge justly, even mercifully.” To a runaway lad he said: “⟦Q 133:4.11⟧Remember, there are two things you cannot run away from—God and yourself.⟦/Q⟧” And to a condemned criminal, in his last hour, he said that while his fellows must judge him by what he had done, “⟦Q 133:4.12⟧there is a Judge to whom you may appeal for forgiveness, and who will judge you by your real motives and better intentions.⟦/Q⟧”
ch15.b022: At last Gonod’s many interests in Corinth were settled, and they prepared to sail for Athens. They traveled in a small boat that could be hauled overland on a track from one of Corinth’s harbors to the other, a distance of ten miles.
ch15.b024: Ganid was thrilled to find himself in the olden center of Greek science and learning, in the cultural heart of the onetime Alexandrian empire, which had once stretched its borders even to his own India. There was little business to do, so Gonod went with the other two to the sights of the city and listened to their discussions.
ch15.b025: One evening at their inn a Greek philosopher talked about science for almost three hours. When he had finished, Jesus spoke. Scientists might some day measure the energy of gravitation, light, and electricity, he said, but they could never scientifically tell what these phenomena are. “⟦Q 133:5.4⟧Science deals with physical-energy activities; religion deals with eternal values. True philosophy grows out of the wisdom which does its best to correlate these quantitative and qualitative observations.⟦/Q⟧” Arithmetic says that if one man can shear a sheep in ten minutes, ten men can shear it in one. “⟦Q 133:5.5⟧That is sound mathematics, but it is not true,⟦/Q⟧” for the ten would get in one another’s way. On the other hand, a social group of human beings working in co-ordinated harmony stands for a force far greater than the simple sum of its parts. “⟦Q 133:5.8⟧The real universe is friendly to every child of the eternal God,⟦/Q⟧” he said, and its unity can be grasped only by conceiving that the quantitative fact and the qualitative value have a common causation in the Paradise Father.
ch15.b026: They were all more than astounded. When the Greek took his leave, he said: “⟦Q 133:5.11⟧At last my eyes have beheld a Jew who thinks something besides racial superiority and talks something besides religion.⟦/Q⟧” Then they retired for the night. Their stay in Athens was pleasant and profitable, but not especially fruitful in human contacts. Too many Athenians of that day were either intellectually proud of the reputation of another age or dull and ignorant, though even then keen minds could still be found among them.
ch16.title: From Ephesus to Mesopotamia
ch16.b002: From Athens the travelers went by way of Troas to Ephesus, the capital of the Roman province of Asia. Many times they walked out to the famous temple of Artemis, about two miles from the city. Artemis was the most famous goddess of all Asia Minor, a perpetuation of the still older mother goddess of ancient Anatolia, and the crude idol displayed in her enormous temple was said to have fallen from heaven. Not all of Ganid’s early training to respect images as symbols of divinity had been erased, and he thought it best to buy a little silver shrine in honor of this fertility goddess. That night the three talked at great length about the worship of things made with human hands.
ch16.b003: On the third day they walked down by the river to watch the dredging of the harbor’s mouth. At noon they fell into conversation with a young Phoenician who was homesick and much discouraged, and who, more than anything, envied a certain young man who had been promoted over his head. Jesus spoke comforting words to him and quoted the olden Hebrew proverb: “⟦Q 133:6.2⟧A man’s gift makes room for him and brings him before great men.⟦/Q⟧” Of all the large cities they visited on this Mediterranean tour, Ephesus was the one where they accomplished least for the later work of the Christian missionaries. Christianity gained its start there largely through Paul, who lived in the city more than two years, making tents for a living and lecturing each night in the main hall of the school of Tyrannus.
ch16.b004: A progressive thinker was connected with this school of philosophy, and Jesus had several profitable sessions with him. In the course of their talks Jesus repeatedly used the word “soul,” until at last the learned Greek asked him what he meant by it. Jesus replied: “⟦Q 133:6.5⟧The soul is the self-reflective, truth-discerning, and spirit-perceiving part of man which forever elevates the human being above the level of the animal world.⟦/Q⟧” Self-consciousness alone is not the soul, he explained; moral self-consciousness is its foundation. Moral choice and spiritual attainment, the ability to know God and the urge to be like him, are the marks of the soul. “⟦Q 133:6.5⟧A stagnant soul is a dying soul.⟦/Q⟧” The divine spirit arrives with the first moral activity of the human mind, and that is the occasion of the soul’s birth. Neither material science nor pure spirit-testing can demonstrate the soul’s existence, yet “⟦Q 133:6.7⟧every morally conscious mortal knows of the existence of his soul as a real and actual personal experience.⟦/Q⟧”
ch16.b006: Before long they set sail for Cyprus, stopping at Rhodes on the way. They enjoyed the long voyage and arrived at the island much rested in body and refreshed in spirit. Since their tour of the Mediterranean was drawing to a close, they planned a period of real rest and play. Landing at Paphos, they at once gathered supplies for several weeks in the near-by mountains, and on the third day they set out for the hills with well-loaded pack animals.
ch16.b007: For two weeks the trio thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Then, without warning, Ganid was taken grievously ill. For two more weeks he suffered from a raging fever and was often delirious. They were far from any human dwelling, and the boy was too sick to be moved, so they nursed him as best they could there in the mountains. Jesus cared for the lad with such skill and tenderness that the father was amazed at the gentleness and adeptness of his every ministry. During Ganid’s three weeks of convalescence Jesus told him many interesting things about nature and her various moods. What fun they had wandering over the mountains together, the boy asking questions, Jesus answering them, and the father marveling at the whole performance.
ch16.b008: In the last week of their stay in the hills, Jesus and Ganid had a long talk on the functions of the human mind. After several hours the lad asked: “⟦Q 133:7.5⟧But, Teacher, what do you mean when you say that man experiences a higher form of self-consciousness than do the higher animals?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered that self-consciousness is a reality, and that ideas are not simply a record of sensations; “⟦Q 133:7.7⟧ideas are sensations plus the reflective interpretations of the personal self; and the self is more than the sum of one’s sensations.⟦/Q⟧” Then he spoke of the divided heart. “⟦Q 133:7.12⟧The human mind does not well stand the conflict of double allegiance. It is a severe strain on the soul to undergo the experience of an effort to serve both good and evil. The supremely happy and efficiently unified mind is the one wholly dedicated to the doing of the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Such peace is not won by seeking peace of mind at any price or by compromising spiritual ideals, but by overcoming evil with the potent force of good. The next day they left for Salamis and took ship for Antioch on the Syrian coast.
ch16.b010: Antioch was the capital of the Roman province of Syria and the residence of the imperial governor. With half a million inhabitants, it was the third city of the empire in size and the first in wickedness and flagrant immorality. Gonod had much business to attend to, so Jesus and Ganid were often alone together. They visited everything in that polyglot city except the grove of Daphne; Gonod and Ganid went to see that notorious shrine of shame, but Jesus declined to go with them. As he drew nearer to Palestine and the end of the journey, he grew sober and reflective. He saw few people in Antioch and seldom went about the city. After much questioning as to why he showed so little interest in the place, Ganid at last induced him to say: “⟦Q 133:8.2⟧This city is not far from Palestine; maybe I shall come back here sometime.⟦/Q⟧”
ch16.b011: Ganid himself had a memorable experience in Antioch. An Indian employed in his father’s business there had become so disgruntled that his dismissal was being considered. When Ganid heard of it, he went to the place of business and held a long conference with his countryman, who felt he had been put at the wrong job. Ganid told him about the Father in heaven and in many ways widened his view of religion. But of all he said, a Hebrew proverb did the most good: “⟦Q 133:8.3⟧Whatsoever your hand finds to do, do that with all your might.⟦/Q⟧”
ch16.b012: From Antioch they went down to Sidon and across to Damascus, and after three days they made ready for the long trek over the desert sands. A caravan journey was nothing new to these well-traveled men. Ganid watched his teacher help load their twenty camels and then volunteer to drive their own animal, and he exclaimed, “⟦Q 133:9.1⟧Teacher, is there anything that you cannot do?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus only smiled and said, “⟦Q 133:9.1⟧The teacher surely is not without honor in the eyes of a diligent pupil.⟦/Q⟧” So they set out for the ancient city of Ur. Jesus was deeply interested in the early history of Ur, the birthplace of Abraham, and equally fascinated by the ruins and traditions of Susa. Gonod and Ganid lengthened their stay three weeks, partly to give him more time for his investigations, and partly in the hope of persuading him to go back to India with them. At Ur Ganid had a long talk with Jesus about the difference between knowledge, wisdom, and truth, and he was greatly charmed by the saying of the Hebrew wise man: “⟦Q 133:9.3⟧Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom. With all your quest for knowledge, get understanding.⟦/Q⟧”
ch16.b014: At last the day of separation came. They were all brave, the lad most of all, but it was a trying ordeal; they were tearful of eye but courageous of heart. In bidding his teacher farewell, Ganid said: “⟦Q 133:9.4⟧Farewell, Teacher, but not forever. When I come again to Damascus, I will look for you. I love you, for I think the Father in heaven must be something like you; at least I know you are much like what you have told me about him. I will remember your teaching, but most of all, I will never forget you.⟦/Q⟧” The father said, “⟦Q 133:9.4⟧Farewell to a great teacher, one who has made us better and helped us to know God.⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus replied, “⟦Q 133:9.4⟧Peace be upon you, and may the blessing of the Father in heaven ever abide with you.⟦/Q⟧”
ch16.b015: Then Jesus stood on the shore and watched as the small boat carried them out across the water to their anchored ship. So the Master left his friends from India at Charax, never to see them again in this world. Nor were they, in this world, ever to know that the man who later appeared as Jesus of Nazareth was the same friend they had just left behind on the beach—Joshua their teacher. In India Ganid grew up to become an influential man, a worthy successor to his eminent father, and he spread abroad many of the noble truths he had learned from his beloved teacher. Later in life, when he heard of a strange teacher in Palestine who had ended his career on a cross, he recognized the likeness between the gospel of this Son of Man and the teachings of his Jewish tutor; but it never occurred to him that the two were actually the same person. Thus ended that chapter in the life of the Son of Man which might be called the mission of Joshua the teacher.
part4: Part Four: The Fullness of Time
ch17.title: The Caspian Caravan and Mount Hermon
ch17.b002: During the Mediterranean journey Jesus had carefully studied the people he met and the countries through which he passed, and at about this time he reached his final decision about the rest of his life on earth. He had fully considered, and now finally approved, the plan that he be born of Jewish parents in Palestine. Through his own human experience he had found that Palestine was the best place in all the Roman world in which to set forth the closing chapters and enact the final scenes of his earthly life. He decided to finish his career in the same land where he had entered human experience as a helpless babe, among the Jews. Of his own free will he returned to Galilee to await the beginning of his lifework as a public teacher of truth.
ch17.b003: After parting from Gonod and Ganid at Charax in December of A.D. 23, Jesus went back by way of Ur to Babylon and joined a desert caravan bound for Damascus. From there he went toward Nazareth, stopping only a few hours at Capernaum to call on Zebedee’s family. There he found his brother James, who had come over some time before to work in his place in Zebedee’s boatshop, and Jude, who chanced to be in town. After talking with them, he turned over to James the little house that John Zebedee had managed to buy for him, and went on to Nazareth. At the end of his journey he had received enough money to meet his living expenses almost up to the beginning of his public ministry. But apart from Zebedee and the people he had met along the way, the world never knew that he had made this journey. His family always believed that he had spent the time studying in Alexandria, and Jesus neither confirmed this belief nor openly denied it.
ch17.b004: In the few weeks he spent at Nazareth, Jesus visited family and friends and worked a little in the repair shop with his brother Joseph, but most of his attention went to Mary and Ruth. Ruth was nearly fifteen, and this was his first chance to have long talks with her since she had become a young woman. Simon and Jude had both wanted to marry for some time, but they would not do so without their eldest brother’s blessing, and so they had waited for his return. In early March of A.D. 24 they were married at a double wedding. Now only Ruth, the youngest, remained at home with Mary. When the family was all together Jesus had so little to say that they remarked on it, and Mary especially was disconcerted by this strange behavior of her first-born son.
ch17.b005: About the time Jesus was preparing to leave Nazareth, the conductor of a large caravan passing through the city was taken violently ill, and Jesus, being a linguist, volunteered to take his place. Since the trip would keep him away for a year, he called a family conference and proposed that his mother and Ruth go to live in Capernaum, in the house he had just given to James. A few days after he left, they moved there, and Mary lived in that home for the rest of her life. Joseph and his family moved into the old Nazareth house. This was one of the more unusual years in the inner experience of the Son of Man. Great progress was made in bringing his human mind and the indwelling Adjuster into working harmony. These were the in-between times, the transition stage of that being who began life as God appearing as man, and who was now making ready to complete his earth career as man appearing as God.
ch17.b007: On the first of April, A.D. 24, Jesus left Nazareth as conductor of the caravan. It was traveling from Jerusalem by way of Damascus and Lake Urmia, through Assyria, Media, and Parthia, to the southeastern region of the Caspian Sea, and a full year passed before he came back. During this year Jesus worked in an executive capacity, responsible for the goods entrusted to him and for the safe conduct of the travelers, and he discharged these duties faithfully, efficiently, and wisely.
ch17.b008: Passengers, guards, and camel drivers became a kind of family around their leader, and scores of men, women, and children living along the route lived richer lives for having met the extraordinary conductor of a commonplace caravan. Not all profited by these meetings, but the great majority of those who talked with him were made better for the rest of their lives. Of all his travels, this one carried Jesus nearest to the Orient. He came into intimate personal contact with every surviving race of Urantia except the red, and he enjoyed ministering to each of them. Europeans from the Far West and Asiatics from the Far East alike listened to his words of hope and eternal life, and all were touched by the life of loving service he lived among them.
ch17.b010: On the way to the Caspian, Jesus had stopped for several days of rest at the old Persian city of Urmia on the western shore of Lake Urmia. On the largest of a group of islands a short way offshore stood a great lecture amphitheater dedicated to the “spirit of religion”—really a temple of the philosophy of religions. It had been built by Cymboyton, a wealthy merchant of Urmia, and his three sons. More than thirty religions and cults were represented on its faculty of about seventy-five teachers, who lived in cottages of a dozen each. Only one doctrine was required for a seat on the faculty: every teacher must represent a religion that recognized God, some sort of supreme Deity. Intolerance or a contentious spirit brought prompt and summary dismissal. Five teachers belonged to no organized religion, and it was as one of these independent teachers that Jesus appeared before them.
ch17.b011: Jesus took part in several discussions, and before he left, Cymboyton arranged for him to stop for two weeks on his return trip, to give twenty-four lectures on “The Brotherhood of Men” and to lead twelve evening sessions of questions and debate. Jesus kept the arrangement. This was the most systematic and formal of all the Master’s teaching on Urantia; never before or after did he say so much on one subject. In reality the lectures were on the “Kingdom of God” and the “Kingdoms of Men.”
ch17.b012: Their foundation was simple. The brotherhood of men is founded on the fatherhood of God. Since God is spirit, his kingdom is spiritual, a spiritual relationship between God and man. As long as different religions recognize the spirit sovereignty of God the Father, they will remain at peace. Only when one religion claims to be superior to all others, and to possess exclusive authority over them, will it dare to be intolerant and to persecute. God alone is spirit sovereign. Spiritually all men are equal; the kingdom of heaven is free from castes, classes, social levels, and economic groups, and all are brethren. The Urmia religionists lived together in comparative peace because they had fully surrendered all their notions of religious sovereignty. The revelators later explained that they had restated these teachings for the religious and political conditions of the twentieth century, applying them also to the problem of the political sovereignty of nations.
ch17.b013: After Cymboyton’s death, his sons found it hard to keep the faculty at peace. The eldest appealed to Abner at Philadelphia for help, but the Christian teachers Abner chose proved unyielding and uncompromising and sought to make their religion dominant over the other beliefs. They never suspected that the oft-quoted lectures of the caravan conductor had been given by Jesus himself. As confusion grew, the three brothers withdrew their support, and after five years the school closed. Later it was reopened as a Mithraic temple and eventually burned down during one of their orgiastic celebrations.
ch17.b014: On the return journey Jesus gave up the direction of the caravan at Lake Urmia, stayed a little over two weeks, and went on as a passenger with a later caravan to Damascus. There the camel owners begged him to remain in their service, but he declined, and he arrived at Capernaum on the first of April, A.D. 25. Nazareth was no longer his home; Capernaum had become the home of Jesus, James, Mary, and Ruth. Yet Jesus never again lived with his family. When in Capernaum he stayed with the Zebedees.
ch17.b016: When Jesus returned from the Caspian, he knew that his world travels were nearly over. He made only one more journey outside Palestine, into Syria. In the middle of April he left Nazareth for Tyre, stayed a few days at Sidon, and went on to Antioch. This was the year of his solitary wanderings through Palestine and Syria, and in different places he was known by different names: the carpenter of Nazareth, the boatbuilder of Capernaum, the scribe of Damascus, the teacher of Alexandria. At Antioch he lived for over two months, working, observing, and ministering, learning how man lives and thinks; for three weeks he worked as a tentmaker. Ten years later, when the Apostle Paul preached in Antioch and heard his followers speak of the doctrines of the Damascus scribe, he little knew that they had heard the voice of the Master himself.
ch17.b017: From Antioch Jesus went south along the coast to Caesarea and Joppa, then inland to Jamnia, Ashdod, and Gaza, and by the inland trail to Beersheba, where he stayed a week. From there he set out on his final tour as a private individual, through the heart of Palestine from Beersheba in the south to Dan in the north. At Bethlehem he saw his birthplace; at Jerusalem he did not visit Bethany; and passing through Samaria, Magdala, and Capernaum, he came at last to Dan, or Caesarea-Philippi. Now the indwelling Thought Adjuster led him away from the dwelling places of men and up to Mount Hermon, that he might finish mastering his human mind and complete his full consecration to the rest of his lifework.
ch17.b019: Near Caesarea-Philippi Jesus gathered his supplies, and with a beast of burden and a lad named Tiglath he went along the Damascus road to a village called Beit Jenn in the foothills of Mount Hermon. There, near the middle of August, A.D. 25, he set up his headquarters, left his supplies with Tiglath, and climbed the lonely slopes. On the first day Tiglath went with him to a point about 6,000 feet above the sea, where they built a stone container in which the boy was to leave food twice a week. After he had left Tiglath, Jesus had climbed only a little way when he stopped to pray. Among other things he asked his Father to send back the guardian seraphim to “be with Tiglath.” He asked to go up alone to his last struggle with the realities of mortal existence, and his request was granted. He went into the great test with only his indwelling Adjuster to guide and sustain him.
ch17.b020: He stayed on the mountain through the last three weeks of August and the first three of September. He ate frugally, going without food only a day or two at a time. During these weeks he finished the mortal task of achieving the circles of mind-understanding and personality-control. After more than five weeks of unbroken communion with his Paradise Father, he became absolutely assured of his nature and of the certainty of his triumph over the material levels of time-space personality manifestation.
ch17.b021: Near the end of his stay he asked his Father whether he might hold conference with his Satania enemies as the Son of Man, as Joshua ben Joseph. The request was granted. During the last week on Mount Hermon the great temptation, the universe trial, took place. Satan, representing Lucifer, and the rebellious Planetary Prince, Caligastia, were present with Jesus and made fully visible to him. They were real beings, his archenemies in the system of Satania, not phantasms of a weakened and starving mind. And this trial had nothing to do with food, temple pinnacles, or presumptuous acts; it had not to do with the kingdoms of this world but with the sovereignty of a mighty and glorious universe. To the many proposals and counterproposals of the emissaries of Lucifer, Jesus only made reply:

ch17.b022.en: “May the will of my Paradise Father prevail, and you, my rebellious son, may the Ancients of Days judge you divinely. I am your Creator-father; I can hardly judge you justly, and my mercy you have already spurned. I commit you to the adjudication of the Judges of a greater universe.”

ch17.b023: To every compromise and makeshift Lucifer suggested, Jesus answered only, “⟦Q 134:8.8⟧The will of my Father in Paradise be done.⟦/Q⟧” When the ordeal was over, the guardian seraphim returned to his side and ministered to him. On an afternoon in late summer, amid the trees and in the silence of nature, Michael of Nebadon won the unquestioned sovereignty of his universe. The universe announcement was not made until the day of his baptism, months later, but it all really took place that day on the mountain. When Jesus came down from Mount Hermon, the Lucifer rebellion in Satania and the Caligastia secession on Urantia were virtually settled. The so-called “great temptation” of Jesus took place before his baptism, not just after it.
ch17.b024: On the way down he met Tiglath coming up with food. Turning him back, he said only: “⟦Q 134:8.10⟧The period of rest is over; I must return to my Father’s business.⟦/Q⟧” He was a silent and much changed man as they walked back to Dan. There he gave the boy the donkey and took his leave, and then went south by the way he had come, to Capernaum.
ch17.b026: It was now near the end of summer, close to the day of atonement and the feast of tabernacles. After a family meeting in Capernaum over the Sabbath, Jesus set out for Jerusalem with John the son of Zebedee, going east of the lake and down the Jordan valley. On the way John noticed a great change in him. They spent a night at Bethany with Lazarus and his sisters, and then almost three weeks in and around Jerusalem. Many days John went into the city alone while Jesus walked the near-by hills in communion with his Father. Both attended the solemn services of the day of atonement. John was deeply impressed, but Jesus stood by, a thoughtful and silent spectator. To the Son of Man it was pitiful and pathetic, a travesty upon the facts of divine justice and the truths of infinite mercy. He burned to declare the real truth about his Father’s loving character, but his faithful Monitor reminded him that his hour had not yet come.
ch17.b027: Midway through the week of the feast of tabernacles, the joyous holiday of all Palestine, Jesus took leave of John, saying that he wished to withdraw to the hills to commune with his Father. John wanted to come, but Jesus insisted that he stay, saying: “⟦Q 134:9.5⟧It is not required of you to bear the burden of the Son of Man; only the watchman must keep vigil while the city sleeps in peace.⟦/Q⟧” After almost a week alone in the hills near Bethany, he started for Capernaum. On the way he spent a day and a night alone on the slopes of Gilboa, near where King Saul had taken his life. When he reached Capernaum, he seemed more cheerful than when he had left John in Jerusalem.
ch17.b028: The next morning he went to the chest of his belongings in Zebedee’s workshop, put on his apron, and presented himself for work, saying, “⟦Q 134:9.6⟧It behooves me to keep busy while I wait for my hour to come.⟦/Q⟧” For several months, until January of the next year, he worked in the boatshop beside his brother James, mostly on the interior finishing of the larger craft, taking great pains with every essential piece of work. After those months together, no matter what doubts later clouded James’s understanding, he never again wholly gave up his faith in the mission of Jesus.
ch17.b029: As time passed, rumors reached Capernaum of one John who was baptizing penitents in the Jordan and preaching: “⟦Q 134:9.8⟧The kingdom of heaven is at hand; repent and be baptized.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus listened to the reports as John slowly worked his way up the Jordan valley, and he went on making boats. A great change had come over him. Few of those who had known him as a private man in his travels up and down the land would ever recognize him in the public teacher of later days, for this long transformation of mind and spirit had been finished during the eventful sojourn on Mount Hermon.
